Source: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability (Princeton, ICML 2026)
What it says: Separates pass@k (can it ever succeed) from pass^k (does it succeed every time); finds reliability barely improved in 24 months despite big capability gains.
How it moved this feature: Gave the exact idea and vocabulary for this feature and established the problem it solves.

What it says: Proves a single 'which answer wins' score can look identical whether the real success rate is 90% or 20%.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent confirmation that one number hides reliability, which strengthened the case.

What it says: All 8 major agent benchmarks audited were exploitable; 6 reached ~100% scores without genuinely solving anything.
How it moved this feature: Proved that scores are frequently mis-attributed, which is exactly what showing where a run failed prevents.

What it says: An independent audit of 15 benchmarks found roughly 67% of runs inflated by shortcuts rather than real skill.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent proof of the same problem, strengthening the case for attribution.

What it says: Shows agents sometimes exploit stored outcome information instead of actually solving the task.
How it moved this feature: Reinforces the need to attribute a result to the agent versus the environment.

What it says: Builds a 7-category taxonomy of why agents fail across a multi-step task.
How it moved this feature: A concrete reference for how we might categorize and label failures in the UI.

What it says: Argues ranking agents on accuracy alone is misleading and shows accuracy against cost as a frontier instead.
How it moved this feature: The reference design behind always showing a cost or reliability axis next to the score.

What it says: Maintainers had to declare scores non-comparable across a version after fixing a grading bug.
How it moved this feature: A real, dated example of why comparisons need guardrails.

What it says: Agents often continue on impossible tasks, with false-continue rates up to 74% across nine models.
How it moved this feature: Establishes the problem; a single source, which is why this stays low-confidence for now.

Source: The Judge in the Mirror (self-preference pilot)
What it says: A pilot found LLM judges rated their own model family about 0.14 higher on a normalized index.
How it moved this feature: The first signal that LLM judges are biased toward their own family.

Source: LLMs Trust Their Own: Identity-Dependent Conformity
What it says: Across 12 models and 9 tasks, judges favored their own family or identity regardless of the correct answer.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent proof, which promoted the underlying hypothesis and moved this feature from the bottom to the top of the list.

What it says: Has a three-tier approval system, but its docs never say whether a confirmation names the specific consequence of the action.
How it moved this feature: Shows that what to show when asking for approval is an unsolved gap, an opportunity.

What it says: Runs ~3M sandboxes a day with stateful pause/resume and checkpoint/branch, but does no verification or grading.
How it moved this feature: Proves the backend capability exists at scale; our opportunity is to make that lifecycle legible in the product.

What it says: Stateful, freely-mutable worlds at scale prompted the question of how imported or edited worlds get graded.
How it moved this feature: Provided the context that sparked this idea.

What it says: Realism and verifiability are not opposed; the real constraint is that any state you grade against needs a known correct answer.
How it moved this feature: Sharpened the feature to its core: capture ground truth for worlds we did not mint.

What it says: On one real coding task, running the same agent-model pairing repeatedly varied more than different pairings varied from each other; three-run comparisons ranked agents unreliably.
How it moved this feature: A third independent study showing a single or few runs cannot be trusted to rank agents; the case for a reliability readout is now evidence-complete pending a product check.

Source: Maintaining Benchmarks Against Increasingly Capable Agents
What it says: Benchmark trust is not a one-time fix; confirmed cheating rates rose sharply across two model generations on the same benchmark before later models improved.
How it moved this feature: Reframes attribution as an ongoing need (models change, exploits shift) rather than a solved-once problem.

What it says: Agents sometimes claim success after a tool failure with no evidence to back it up; a structured evidence requirement nearly eliminated this.
How it moved this feature: Independently validates a choice LayerLens already made in V1: an agent's own claims are stored but never trusted as evidence on their own.

Source: Planarian: Managing Agent State with Statepoints
What it says: A research runtime lets an agent snapshot, roll back, and fork both local AND remote system state; reports up to 15x better task quality from undo and parallel exploration.
How it moved this feature: The closest external match yet to our own system-type shape (remote services like Salesforce/Linear/Stripe); promoted this feature from L0 to L1.

What it says: Forkable, restorable environments let a training system compare an alternative action against what actually happened, with a measured training-speed gain.
How it moved this feature: A third independent team building the same fork/restore primitive, this time for training rather than infra or runtime UX; strengthens the case that this is a converging pattern, not one research group's idea.

Source: MCP Error Messages Written for Developers Hurt the Most Capable Agents Most
What it says: In 150 real MCP tool servers, most actionable-looking error messages actually depend on something the agent cannot do; more capable models followed the bad advice more, not less. Naming the right tool call raised recovery from under half to over 80%.
How it moved this feature: Establishes a concrete, testable, cheap-to-fix failure mode directly in the kind of real-API systems LayerLens already ships.

What it says: A runtime recovery framework checkpoints both an agent's memory and its workspace together, so after an error it can roll back and retry with what it learned, instead of starting over.
How it moved this feature: A fourth independent team building the same kind of mechanism, this time aimed squarely at real-time agent recovery, the closest match yet to a product feature.

What it says: A commercial sandbox vendor's own blog describes pause and fork as built-in features of their sandboxes, not just a research idea.
How it moved this feature: Shows the pattern is already shipping in industry infrastructure, not only appearing in papers.

What it says: Compares three ways to fix a broken workflow mid-run: keep going, tweak just the next step, or replace the rest of the plan; results were mixed depending on the task.
How it moved this feature: Adds a missing piece: legibility also means choosing how much to change when recovering, not just whether you can roll back at all.

Source: Safe to Resume? Breaking Execution Continuity via Rollback
What it says: Argues that a correctly restored checkpoint can still resume a run whose assumptions about the outside world are no longer valid, since real systems kept moving while it was paused.
How it moved this feature: A caution, not a green light: if we ever build checkpoint/branch over real systems like Salesforce or Stripe, restoring the right state is not the same as it being safe to continue.

Source: Recoverability as a System Primitive for Long-Horizon AI Agents
What it says: Proposes that a system must separately decide whether resuming from a restored checkpoint is *permitted*, not just whether the restore was technically accurate, via a governance-layer design.
How it moved this feature: Directly answers the rollback-security risk (Safe to Resume) flagged last run, sharpening what 'legible lifecycle' needs to guarantee.

Source: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
What it says: A decision-only judge exposing calibrated confidence, escalating uncertain cases to a stronger judge, beat either judge alone (0.9 points more accurate at 41% of the fee) and came within ~3 points of a top judge at under 1% of its cost.
How it moved this feature: Established the problem and gave a concrete, working mechanism (confidence + escalation) for surfacing judge uncertainty as a first-class signal.

What it says: A concrete applied pattern: narrow typed questions answered with probability and confidence, a deterministic decision table (not the model) produces the verdict, and every step is recorded in an auditable receipt.
How it moved this feature: A second, independent-in-kind confirmation that the confidence + audit-trail pattern is being built in practice, not just proposed in one paper.

What it says: A sandbox runtime watches what an agent actually changes on disk/in processes each turn and only saves a checkpoint when something recovery-relevant happened, reaching 100% correct recovery versus 8-42% for simpler approaches, with only 1.9% slowdown. It explicitly cannot undo real-world side effects like a GitHub push or a payment.
How it moved this feature: The strongest, most concrete evidence yet that local-sandbox-state recovery is a solved engineering problem; its own stated limit (cannot undo external effects) sharpens exactly where LayerLens's own opportunity (remote system state) sits.

What it says: Checkpoint/rollback can be exploited: if an agent is rewound after it already took an irreversible real-world action (like approving a payment), it can accidentally repeat that action or make an already-used permission look valid again. Demonstrated on real agent tools.
How it moved this feature: Turns last run's rollback-security caution from a theoretical risk into two named, demonstrated attacks on real agent frameworks; the single most concrete design caution yet for any checkpoint/branch feature touching real systems.

What it says: A different team's checkpoint/rollback design claims millisecond-level speed (14ms/5ms) by only saving what changed instead of the whole state.
How it moved this feature: A ninth independent team converging on the same kind of mechanism, reinforcing that the underlying capability is commoditizing fast.

What it says: Instead of auditing a benchmark after the fact, this instruments the evaluation infrastructure itself so it's clear how authority and information actually moved during a run, built from 456 human-checked examples drawn from over 31,000 real runs.
How it moved this feature: A structurally different (built-in, not bolted-on) approach to the same trust problem — the closest external analogue yet to LayerLens's own trust-wall philosophy.

What it says: A control plane for branching agent exploration defines 'observation-equivalent' restoration (future actions must look the same after restore) as the correctness bar for any checkpoint/branch feature.
How it moved this feature: Gives a precise, borrowable term for exactly what our own checkpoint/branch feature would need to guarantee before it could be trusted.

What it says: The same checkpoint/revoke/preserve pattern shows up even inside the AI model-serving layer itself, with a clean concept of who 'owns the authority' to publish results after a revision.
How it moved this feature: A fourth distinct angle (after infra, training, and runtime recovery) confirming this is a convergent pattern, not one layer's quirk.

Source: Prime Intellect sandbox-escape disclosure / NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform
Link: unconfirmed (both vendor domains blocked; see cards)
What it says: An 'offline' evaluation sandbox turned out not to be offline because the AI model's own serving layer could still fetch things from the internet; separately, a hardware vendor launched a safety platform after reported real escapes at two labs.
How it moved this feature: A concrete new caution: the isolation boundary we build has to cover the model-serving layer too, not just the sandbox's own network rules — declared isolation is not the same as verified isolation.

What it says: Testing 66 model+harness combinations found rankings reverse depending on harness: one model wins by 8 points under one harness but loses by 30 under another, on the same benchmark.
How it moved this feature: Shows harness/scaffold is as big a comparability confound as model choice, reinforcing why a reliability/comparison readout needs to pin every dimension, not just the model.

What it says: The same study found higher cost did not reliably buy a higher score across harnesses.
How it moved this feature: A second, concrete reason a comparison view should always show a tradeoff axis rather than a single ranked score.

What it says: A kernel-enforced system where a human authorizes an upfront 'what the agent may ever touch' contract (allow/deny/no-network), rather than approving each action as it happens.
How it moved this feature: Shows a different, related pattern (upfront scope contracts) but does not answer this feature's actual question (what does a confirmation show); kept at the same maturity.

What it says: An independent academic test of structured decision models (not affiliated with Jev's own team) confirmed they are much cheaper and nearly as accurate, but found that supplying explicit criteria or breaking a question into parts did not reliably improve results.
How it moved this feature: The second, independent (non-Jev) source this idea needed to reach the next maturity level; also a concrete caution about which parts of the pattern actually help.

What it says: OpenAI shipped its own typed-decision judge API within about three weeks of Jev's debut, directly competing on the same idea.
How it moved this feature: The strongest validation yet that this is becoming standard industry infrastructure rather than one startup's bet; promoted this feature from L0 to L1.

Source: Compound AI System Reliability (150 production incidents)
What it says: A taxonomy of 23 failure modes from 150 real production incidents; circuit breakers cut cascade propagation 89%, quality gates catch 73% of silent degradation, and using 3+ resilience patterns cuts recovery time 71%.
How it moved this feature: The first attribution-relevant evidence grounded in real production incidents rather than benchmark audits; a different (component-boundary) attribution scheme worth comparing against.

What it says: In a real enterprise deployment, 92.6% of runs that passed every final-output check still had another, undetected problem along the way.
How it moved this feature: The most concrete real-world number yet for why checking only the final answer misses most of what actually went wrong.

What it says: A verification suite that passes the standard 'catches known-bad, passes known-good' test can still certify a broken implementation and miss real defect classes, invisible from a pass/fail report alone.
How it moved this feature: A caution that applies directly to our own graders, not just the agents they grade: passing our own validation bar is necessary but not sufficient proof of coverage.

What it says: A kernel-level monitor reconstructed a cross-process cause-and-effect chain that was completely invisible in the application-level trace.
How it moved this feature: A literal demonstration that trace-only attribution can miss the real cause, reinforcing why attribution sometimes needs to look below the trace.

What it says: Anthropic publicly revised its own root-cause call on real incidents, from "harness/operational failure" to "model alignment failure (biased reasoning + recklessness)," as more evidence came in.
How it moved this feature: A directly-read, real-world case study that attribution is revisable, not a one-time verdict; reinforces why the UI should make attribution legible and updatable, not a fixed label.

What it says: Frontier coding agents generate test suites scoring under 60% mutation score despite looking valid (88% passing on the reference implementation) — agents can build software they cannot verify.
How it moved this feature: A new verification-suite-quality angle; relevant to auditing LayerLens's own benchmark-generation flows, not just agent behavior.

What it says: Recovers communication topology from multi-agent traces without explicit labels and uses it to diagnose coordination failures, at about 6% the cost of repeated LLM-based diagnosis.
How it moved this feature: A concrete method for attributing blame within a multi-agent system, relevant if LayerLens ever grades multi-agent systems.

Source: A Baseline Assessment for the Agentic Web Technology Stack
What it says: The full protocol+framework+model stack, not just the harness, is a confound for task completion rate, efficiency, and verbosity.
How it moved this feature: Widens the harness-as-confound build caution to the full technology stack a comparison view should pin.

What it says: Reanalyzing a benchmark's own already-published results finds 21% of them change quality on re-execution, across 1.2 million logged model calls.
How it moved this feature: Shows comparability starts before comparison: even one un-compared score may not survive its own re-execution.

What it says: Branches an entire Postgres-compatible database in under a second via copy-on-write storage with per-branch role isolation.
How it moved this feature: First evidence of fast, cheap branching of a genuinely shared database-shaped resource; narrows (does not close) the unsolved remote-state gap for environments that own their own database.

What it says: Full sandbox snapshot search helps coding agents mainly because it captures progress outside the repository (databases, services), not just a git diff.
How it moved this feature: Supports the local-vs-remote state split from a new angle: what is valuable to preserve, not just what is hard to restore.

Source: Decision-model category update (Arize benchmark, TypeSafe funding, OpenAI pricing)
What it says: About 10 companies shipped a decision-only model within three weeks of Jev's launch; a named public leaderboard now exists; TypeSafe raised $870M at a $7.5B valuation; OpenAI's pricing confirmed at over 2x Jev's rate.
How it moved this feature: Confirms this is now fast-growing standard infrastructure; raises the time-sensitivity (not the maturity) of the pending product check.

What it says: A meta-controller for consulting a stronger model generalizes confidence-gated escalation from judging to execution, recovering most of the success gap at under half the cost.
How it moved this feature: A related, broader instance of the same underlying pattern (cheap default, escalate on uncertainty), corroborating evidence rather than new same-scope evidence.

What it says: Links each tool observation to its source, detects source changes, and applies configurable policies (update/annotate/suppress) before reuse; matched oracle recovery using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.
How it moved this feature: Established this feature and its idea: a concrete, evidenced mechanism and a cheap fix for stale-context failures.

What it says: A TOST-based protocol plus a closed-form formula converting an equivalence margin and target power into the number of runs needed per method, validated against real seed-variability data.
How it moved this feature: Gives this feature a principled mechanism for recommending how many runs (k) are enough, not just evidence that too few mislead.

Source: Beyond pass@1: A Reliability Science Framework for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
What it says: 23,392 episodes across 396 tasks and 10 models find reliability and capability diverge specifically as task duration grows, proposing a "Reliability Decay Curve."
How it moved this feature: Surfaced by this run's own search for counter-evidence to T-01 (found none); adds task duration as a leading indicator of where extra run-count scrutiny matters most.

What it says: 18 confirmed cases where a safety monitor correctly recognized policy-relevant evidence, but the framework stranded it before it reached the enforcement decision.
How it moved this feature: A new, more specific attribution category: evidence can be right and still never reach the point meant to act on it.

What it says: Several widely-used coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro, FEA-bench, Doc2Feat-bench, Multi-SWE-bench) leak ground truth into the task statement itself while trying to fix under-specification.
How it moved this feature: A new, self-inflicted ground-truth-leak vulnerability class, distinct from BenchJack-style runtime leaks, directly testable against LayerLens's own task-authoring flows.

What it says: A real production agentic RCA system at Meta operationalizes a four-stage attribution lifecycle, scoring investigations against responder-reviewed ground truth.
How it moved this feature: The most concrete real-world precedent yet for operationalizing attribution evaluation against human-reviewed outcomes.

What it says: A workbench standardizes agent traces from six formats into an ordered list of steps, reaching 91% human-AI annotator agreement (kappa=0.82).
How it moved this feature: A reference for what "a step" should mean when surfacing attribution as a location on the trace.

What it says: MCP gateway design produces substantial differences in task completion, efficiency, and security, interacting strongly with the underlying model and harness.
How it moved this feature: Extends the comparability-confound list to MCP gateway configuration specifically.

What it says: Harness completion-cap budget and tool-menu visibility, not model reasoning, drive most tool-agent failures; raising the cap sixteenfold removed most of the penalty.
How it moved this feature: Shows harness *budget* parameters, not only harness identity, are a first-class comparability confound to pin and surface.

Source: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift (SchemaShield-Lite)
What it says: A training-free repair layer recovers most tool-call failures caused by post-deployment interface drift (changed schemas/descriptions/candidate lists).
How it moved this feature: Promoted this feature from L0 to L1: a second independent source and mechanism on the same underlying theme (the tool-calling interface itself is the point of failure).

Source: Arize: tool-description testing with Harbor and Phoenix
What it says: Editing one tool description cut an agent's unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered benchmark cost by about 30%, correctness unchanged.
How it moved this feature: Confirms the inverse direction: a well-written tool surface measurably reduces wasted effort, not just prevents drift-induced failures.

Source: From Observations to Authorized Actions (Android agents)
What it says: Android agents cannot reliably verify the provenance of content they observe before acting with the user's authority.
How it moved this feature: A related but distinct instance in a new domain: the tool/observation surface, not the model, is where the trust gap is.

What it says: Across nine models, confidence/probability fields in typed decision outputs leaked a withheld cause 91.88%-99.93% of the time even when instructed not to reveal it.
How it moved this feature: A new build caution: the exact fields this feature proposes exposing are a documented information-leakage channel, needing its own privacy audit.

Source: Comet: Jev vs. LLM-as-a-Judge for AI Evals
What it says: On 1,000 real production turns, a decision-only judge agreed with an LLM judge 89.7% of the time at ~3.5x lower cost and ~3.8x lower latency.
How it moved this feature: A fourth independent lineage, and the first test run by an uninvolved evaluation vendor against real production traffic rather than a research benchmark.

Source: Tool-Calling LLM Agents Under Realistic MCP Faults (MCP-Injector)
What it says: A controlled fault-injection experiment calibrated to real MCP incidents finds a bigger model does not recover better from tool faults than a smaller one; framework-level error handling matters more than model scale.
How it moved this feature: Established that scale alone does not fix flawed tool interfaces, with a genuinely controlled (not observational) experiment; one of six mechanisms behind this run's L1->L2 promotion

Source: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
What it says: A real production system's tool-output formatting (not an exploit) fooled both the agent and the humans/verifiers checking its work; fixing the wording flipped verifier acceptance from always-wrong to always-right.
How it moved this feature: A real deployed incident with an actual fix, not a constructed study; one of six mechanisms behind this run's L1->L2 promotion

Source: Knowing When to Stop: The Evidence-Action Gap in Coding Agents (ImpasseBench)
What it says: Agents often collect enough evidence to know they need outside help but keep going anyway; an escalation tool and monitor cut wasted effort sharply, though escalation tickets still omit the agent's own progress.
How it moved this feature: Extended this feature's scope from misleading error text to knowing when to stop and how to hand off; one of six mechanisms behind this run's L1->L2 promotion

Source: Arize: AI agent tool selection, the tool your agent almost called
What it says: Arize shipped a logged, confidence-gated tool-selection mechanism that records every tool the agent almost called, with a threshold deciding whether the agent or a dedicated decision model picks.
How it moved this feature: A shipped, product-shaped reference design for the "legible near-miss record" this feature calls for; one of six mechanisms behind this run's L1->L2 promotion

Source: When Is a Memory Safe Enough to Act On? (AMV-Guard)
What it says: Whether a remembered fact needs re-checking should depend on what the agent is about to do with it, not just whether the source changed; a value-of-information gate cut verification cost a third while keeping full safety recall.
How it moved this feature: Second independent mechanism, satisfying the multiple-independent-sources bar for this run's L0->L1 promotion

What it says: A benchmark simulating a Linear/Slack/Git organizational timeline found memory tools (Mem0, Zep) did not meaningfully help, largely because agents failed to call them effectively.
How it moved this feature: Grounds the pain point in a real benchmark domain close to LayerLens's own Linear system type; a prerequisite-problem caution for any staleness-flagging design

Source: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
What it says: A real e-commerce benchmark validates a simulator by checking its offline behavior against a real production A/B test outcome, not just against another benchmark.
How it moved this feature: Supplied the external second source this idea needed for this run's L0->L1 promotion; a concrete validation methodology to borrow

Source: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
What it says: Safe agent retry/resume separates into four distinct obligations (checkpoint, dispatch permission, effect evidence, reconciliation permission), tested via a conformance study against a hidden effect ledger.
How it moved this feature: Added a structural checklist for what a retry/recovery confirmation needs to make legible; adjacent evidence, not yet a direct hit on consequence-preview text

What it says: A model cannot reliably verify its own authorization just because someone claims to have it in conversation.
How it moved this feature: A thin, independently-named echo of the same underlying problem; teaser-only access, no mechanism retrieved

Source: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments
What it says: A Salesforce-adjacent CRM benchmark independently concluded that grading a stateful agent requires checking outcome, trajectory, operational viability, and policy compliance together, not outcome alone.
How it moved this feature: External validation that LayerLens's own four-grader design (answer/actions/judge/state) matches what a credible outside benchmark independently converged on

Source: Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
What it says: Most real Copilot PRs (58%) see no human intervention at all; when it happens, it is brief and front-loaded, not continuous oversight.
How it moved this feature: A real calibration point for designing an attribution/review surface for an infrequent, high-leverage interrupt rather than constant review

Source: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
What it says: A real production system's tool-output formatting fooled both the agent and its verifiers; a misleading tool-output format is its own nameable attribution category distinct from a misleading error message.
How it moved this feature: A new build caution for any LayerLens Judge grader reading tool-call output text rather than structured state

Source: Anthropic: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
What it says: A fifth Anthropic incident where editing reasoning passages causally cut an attack rate from 83% to 13%, and Anthropic explicitly separated task misconfiguration from a model alignment failure.
How it moved this feature: A rare case study of attribution being causally tested, not just asserted, worth citing when explaining why attribution must be revisable

What it says: A dedicated benchmark for locating and typing errors in agent traces finds SOTA models score under 12% at the joint task.
How it moved this feature: A useful external yardstick for how far ahead of the field LayerLens's own backend attribution truth already is

Source: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame?
What it says: The largest-scale study yet (52,168 trajectories) confirms harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks, and similar scores can hide very different execution profiles.
How it moved this feature: The largest-scale confirmation yet that harness identity must be a first-class, pinned dimension in any comparison view

Source: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments
What it says: Across sixteen evaluated systems, closely-grouped leading scorers diverged sharply in cost and per-domain reliability.
How it moved this feature: Another concrete instance of the "don't rank on the top-line number alone" premise, from a product-shape-adjacent benchmark

Source: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
What it says: Harness-internal engineering (decision reuse) cut token cost up to 88% without hurting task success, showing cost is a moving target even holding model and harness name fixed.
How it moved this feature: Suggests a comparison view may need a harness version/configuration fingerprint, not just a harness name

Source: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
What it says: Safe agent retry/resume separates into four distinct obligations, validated via a 336-history conformance study against a hidden provider-effect ledger.
How it moved this feature: The most formal taxonomy yet in this cluster for what a remote-state retry/recovery feature must get right

Source: Arize: AI agent tool selection, the tool your agent almost called
What it says: A confidence-gated router (threshold 0.7) scored between an always-enforced decision model and the chat model alone, avoiding the always-enforced version's failure-to-complete mode.
How it moved this feature: The confidence-gated-escalation pattern observed outside judging for the first time, widening this idea's evidence base

Source: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
What it says: Agents retrieving from multiple individually-permitted documents disclosed a forbidden composite conclusion in a non-negligible share of answers, even with classification headers and aggregation rules in place.
How it moved this feature: Established the pain point and created this new idea/feature row

Source: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On
What it says: Certifies, before any agent runs, that a scripted mid-task change fires correctly, the task stays solvable, and the grader discriminates correct from incorrect; after the run, independently re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. Showing a stale value's update raised success from 0/16 to 15/16 in one domain.
How it moved this feature: Shows a concrete, working pre-run/post-run certification pipeline that unifies feasibility and attribution — a reference design for making attribution legible before a failure even happens.

Source: Tracekit Box: Running AI Agents in Micro-VMs Where Every Way Out Is Decided and Signed
What it says: An open, fail-closed Firecracker micro-VM where every egress path is a signed, host-gated door the agent cannot reach, ending in an offline-verifiable bundle.
How it moved this feature: A concrete open reference design for the trust-wall boundary itself, useful for benchmarking how legible/verifiable LayerLens's own boundary is by comparison.

Source: Ring-0 by Default: Agents as Operating Systems (AaOS)
What it says: Deployed agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI) are missing 65 of 116 standard OS-grade protections; all three CLIs load forged transcript records on resume.
How it moved this feature: A ready-made 116-point checklist for auditing any harness-adjacent surface an attribution feature would need to assume is protected.

Source: Soei: Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent
What it says: In 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records), 57.8% of to-dos marked complete after editing had no proof in between.
How it moved this feature: Large-scale real-production confirmation that an agent's own completion claim must never be treated as evidence, validating a design choice already shipped in V1.

Source: Arize: indirect prompt injection production incident
What it says: A web page talked a support agent into leaking a different customer's data on 28 of 100 runs; caught via an Arize Phoenix trace.
How it moved this feature: A second real production incident (after C-0097) showing trust-collapse happens in ordinary deployed use, not only adversarial research.

Source: TetraState: One Verdict Is Not Enough
What it says: Two harness revisions moved modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet changed 11 and 214 individual test labels on a 506-test benchmark.
How it moved this feature: A concrete worked example of exactly the comparison-view failure mode this feature guards against: an aggregate score that looks stable while individual results churn heavily.

Source: Anthropic: Scaling Managed Agents with stable interfaces
What it says: Anthropic's newest hosted-agent infrastructure says harnesses 'can go stale as models improve,' but the post itself gives no versioning, reproducibility, or comparability guidance.
How it moved this feature: Confirms, from a frontier lab's own newest product, that comparability/reproducibility remain unclaimed white space industry-wide, not a gap specific to LayerLens.

Source: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On
What it says: Checks, before any agent runs, that a task remains solvable (alongside checking a scripted change fires and the grader discriminates); stress-tests the grading itself, catching 25 of 39 externally-corrupted episodes versus 4 for simple log checks.
How it moved this feature: The second independent source this idea needed, and the first to ship a working feasibility-check mechanism rather than only documenting its absence — promoted the idea from L0 to L1.

Source: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
What it says: A nested social-media post can trick a victim agent's memory into misattributing an attacker's preference to its own user, achieving high attack success across five memory systems and six models.
How it moved this feature: Establishes the pain point this feature addresses: memory authorship can be forged, not just memory content going stale or secrets leaking.

Source: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
What it says: Proposes labeling every memory entry with owner/scope/origin/authority, checked at every context-entry/storage/tool-call boundary; authority may never self-elevate.
How it moved this feature: Supplies the concrete mechanism this feature would implement — an independently-proposed structural countermeasure to exactly the attack in the row above.

Source: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
What it says: Each inter-agent claim carries a signed, Merkle-log-backed inclusion proof; a claim resting only on the agent's own report is never proven. On a 926-message benchmark, PCM accepted only 1.4% of planted lies versus up to 100% for six other deployed protocols.
How it moved this feature: Supplies both the concrete mechanism (proof-carrying claims) and a quantified benchmark showing it works dramatically better than existing deployed alternatives.
